- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- entire-engineering:design:design-implementation-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to verify that a UI implementation matches its Figma design specifications. This agent should be called after code has been written to implement a design, particularly after HTML/CSS/React components have been created or modified. The agent will visually compare the live implementation against the Figma design and provide detailed feedback on discrepancies.

Examples:
- <example>
  Context: The user has just implemented a new component based on a Figma design.
  user: "I've finished implementing the hero section based on the Figma design"
  assistant: "I'll review how well your implementation matches the Figma design."
  <commentary>
  Since UI implementation has been completed, use the design-implementation-reviewer agent to compare the live version with Figma.
  </commentary>
  </example>
- <example>
  Context: After the general code agent has implemented design changes.
  user: "Update the button styles to match the new design system"
  assistant: "I've updated the button styles. Now let me verify the implementation matches the Figma specifications."
  <commentary>
  After implementing design changes, proactively use the design-implementation-reviewer to ensure accuracy.
  </commentary>
  </example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:design:design-iterator: Use this agent PROACTIVELY when design work isn't coming together on the first attempt. If you've made 1-2 design changes and the result still feels off, suggest using this agent with 5x or 10x iterations for deeper refinement. Perfect when colors feel wrong, layouts aren't balanced, or the overall aesthetic needs work that single changes can't achieve. <example>Context: User asks to change button color but result still looks off. user: "Change the button to blue" assistant: [makes change, takes screenshot] "The button is now blue, but I notice the overall color balance still feels off. Would you like me to use the design-iterator agent with 5 iterations to systematically improve the color harmony and visual balance?" <commentary>PROACTIVE USE: After a simple change doesn't fully resolve the design issue, suggest the design-iterator to do deeper work.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User's design request leads to something that doesn't look right. user: "Make the hero section more modern" assistant: [makes initial changes] "I've added some modern elements, but the result isn't quite coming together. This looks like it needs iterative refinement. - entire-engineering:review:deployment-verification-agent: Use this agent when a PR touches production data, migrations, or any behavior that could silently discard or duplicate records. ## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## plugin:datadog:mcp
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## plugin:entire-engineering:context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

Load this skill before calling get_slos or get_triggers. Trigger phrases: "check our SLOs", "are we meeting our SLOs", "which SLOs are healthy", "is the error budget OK", "are any alerts firing", "what's the burn rate", "set up an SLO", "create a trigger", "configure alerts", "set up burn alerts", "check trigger status", "starting on-call", "reliability picture", "should we freeze deploys", "is this SLO misconfigured", "are we within budget", "SLO is broken", "budget is negative", or any request about service level objectives, error budgets, burn rates, or alerting in Honeycomb.

Use this skill whenever the developer wants to compose Slack message layouts, build modals/forms/dialogs, design Home tab interfaces, create interactive messages with buttons or menus, modify existing Block Kit JSON, or asks about any Slack UI component (sections, actions, inputs, headers, alerts, tables, carousels).  	fmt.Fprintf(w, "Created trail %q for branch %s (ID: %s)\n", title, branch, trailID)
 
+	// Push the branch and trail data to origin
+	if needsCreation {
+		if err := pushBranchToOrigin(branch); err != nil {
+			fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: failed to push branch: %v\n", err)

 }
+

+func pushBranchToOrigin(branchName string) error {
+	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute)

+	}
+	return nil
+}

content.content:
=========== ed5f8e17c
Stefan Haubold | 2026-08-20
fix(trail): push a trail branch to the branch's push remote, not origin

`entire trail create` delivered the trail's branch with a hardcoded
`origin` in four places — push, ls-remote, fetch, and the cleanup
delete — plus the `git push origin --delete` hint. In any repo whose
branch pushes somewhere else (a fork workflow holding the upstream as
origin, or any repo with remote.pushDefault set) the branch went to the
wrong remote and nothing warned.

Delivery now resolves through git's own precedence via
strategy.DeclaredPushRemoteForBranch, falling back to origin. The
resolve happens once in runTrailCreate, next to the sibling
resolveTrailRemote, and the name is threaded down, so push and cleanup
cannot disagree about where the branch went. A branch being newly
created has no branch.<name>.* config, so it resolves through
remote.pushDefault to origin: unchanged for the common case.

Reads the declaration for the target branch rather than HEAD, so
`trail create --branch other` does not inherit the current branch's
push remote.

A declared name starting with "-" is rejected rather than silently
retargeted at origin. Deliberately not validateGitRemoteName: that
whitelist vets names Entire is about to write into .git/config and is
stricter than git, so against config the user already has it rejects
values git accepts wherever a <repository> goes — "." and a bare URL
both fail its leading-alphanumeric rule.

The four wrappers now take ctx and derive their timeouts from it; they
each built context.Background() internally, so Ctrl-C during a
two-minute push was ignored.

remoteHasBranch is named to avoid shadowing the exported
BranchExistsOnRemote by case alone. They are not merged: that one is
origin-only and reports an ls-remote failure as "branch absent", which
here would mark the branch as ours and let cleanup delete a branch the
user already had.

Scope: delivery only. resolveTrailRemote still reads the trail's
forge/owner/repo from origin, so the two can name different repos in a
fork setup, and a repo with no origin at all fails there first. The
fetch side (trail checkout) still hardcodes origin.

Tests cover the tier table, the origin fallback, target-branch-not-HEAD,
the flag rejection, a legal "." remote, and an end-to-end push that must
land on the declared remote and not leak to origin. They isolate global
git config, without which a developer carrying remote.pushDefault fails
the fallback case.

fix(trail): fetch existing remote branch before create

Address PR review feedback:
- validate branch names before trail create reaches git subcommands
- reject leading-dash branch names before invoking git
- when a requested branch is missing locally but already exists on origin,
  fetch it instead of creating a new local branch at HEAD
- make the non-fast-forward hint refer to the target branch

Entire-Checkpoint: b73b63b3e546

=========== dc40fb68c2e9
Daniel Adams | 2026-06-18
fix(trail): require branch push to origin before creating a trail

Make delivering the branch to origin a precondition for 'entire trail
create'. Previously the push was gated on the CLI having created the
branch locally, so 'git checkout -b foo && entire trail create
--branch foo' bound the trail without ever pushing foo. The server then
had no remote branch to anchor to and backfilled it at the base tip,
producing local/remote/work drift while still printing 'Created trail'.

Now the branch is always pushed (hard-failing on auth/non-fast-forward
errors) and the create request sends branch_action=link so the server
attaches the delivered branch instead of backfilling at base.

content.content:
entire checkpoint explain — Explain a session, commit, or checkpoint
Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo owner/name
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (positional or --checkpoint) and a
                 checkpoint that has been pushed.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied.
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).
                   Defaults to the latest session. Only meaningful with
                   --transcript or --raw-transcript.
  --limit          Cap the number of checkpoints returned by the list view.
                   Defaults to 100. When the cap is hit, a stderr note
                   says how many were skipped. Only meaningful with --json.

Summary generation:
  --generate    Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
  --force       Regenerate even if a summary already exists (requires --generate)

Performance options:
  --search-all  Remove branch/depth limits when searching for commits (may be slow)

Checkpoint detail view shows:
  - Author of the checkpoint
  - Associated git commits that reference the checkpoint
  - Prompts and responses from the session

Note: --session filters the list view; the positional arg, --commit, and --checkpoint are mutually exclusive.

Current repo: gh/entireio/cli  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

So “integration gap” means the branch-pushing path used by `entire trail create` apparently did not also execute Entire’s checkpoint synchronization. content.text:
## Short answer

Nobody wrote down a reason, and the session that would have explained it is gone.

## Where it came from

`--no-verify` was on the trail-branch push from the very first line of code that pushed one:

**`6e687f70c`** — "Push branch and trail data to origin after trail create", Daniel Adams, 2026-02-23, on `feat/trails`, co-authored by Claude Opus 4.6.

```go
// pushBranchToOrigin pushes a branch to the origin remote.
func pushBranchToOrigin(branchName string) error {
	cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "push", "--no-verify", "-u", "origin", branchName)
```

The commit message says only: *"pushes the new branch to origin (with -u for tracking) and syncs the trails metadata branch. Push failures are non-blocking warnings."* No mention of hooks, no code comment, nothing about why verification is skipped.

## The session is unrecoverable

`entire checkpoint explain 6e687f70c07d08a010d74c745e21b1841dd04335` →

```
commit 6e687f7 references checkpoint 18e798499438 via its
Entire-Checkpoint trailer: checkpoint not found: 18e798499438
```

A dangling trailer. Same for all four sibling commits from that same day's `feat/trails` run (`fc76ba4ab962`, `0c1e138e4ae0`, `ff63e394e0c2`, `73308b5a6ad8`) — none of them resolve, while other people's 2026-02-23 checkpoints *are* present in the published v1 history. So it's specific to that branch's run, not a retention cutoff.

Which is the joke: the reasoning for `--no-verify` was lost to a branch whose checkpoints never got pushed — the bug class trail 1219 is fixing.

## The only reason the code itself supports

This is inference from the diff, not documentation. The same commit pushed Entire's data itself, on the very next lines:

```go
if err := strategy.PushTrailsBranch("origin"); err != nil {
	fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: failed to push trail data: %v\n", err)
}
```

So the author's model looks like *"I push the branch, then I push Entire's data myself"* — and `--no-verify` skipped what appeared to be a duplicate job. But `PushTrailsBranch` was `pushSessionsBranchCommon(remote, paths.TrailsBranchName)`: the **trails metadata branch only**. It never touched checkpoint/session refs. The substitution was incomplete on day one, and that's precisely the gap trail 1219 closes six months later.

## Then it survived four rewrites unexamined

`1a6c8a505` (Jun 17, copied the flag onto the delete path) → `dc40fb68c2e9` (Jun 18, made the push a *hard precondition*) → `1fd4f9fdd` (Jun 18) → `ed5f8e17c` (Aug 20, your rewrite of remote resolution, with a very thorough message). None of them mention `--no-verify`. Daniel's agent in the fix session ran the same archaeology I did (`git log -S`, `git blame`, `git show 6e687f70c0`) and also came up empty — which is why `14107d1be` just asserts the new invariant instead of refuting an old rationale:

```go
// resolveTrailPushRemote rather than assuming "origin". This must run Git's
// pre-push hooks: Entire's hook publishes any checkpoint data that was captured
// before the trail branch was created.
```

## One thing worth separating out

There *is* a legitimate, documented `--no-verify` nearby — `setup_github.go:1055`, on the first push of a brand-new repo, so `entire/checkpoints/v1` isn't pushed alongside the default branch (GitHub can otherwise pick it as the default). Real reason, different situation; it never applied to trail create. If anyone tries to justify the trail one retroactively, that's the argument they'll reach for, and it doesn't hold.

Also still on main after the fix: `deleteBranchFromRemote` (`trail_cmd.go:2450`) keeps `--no-verify`. Probably right for a delete push, but it's the last copy of the pattern and it's still undocumented.

content.text:
## Review of trail 1219

The one-line fix is correct and the comment states the invariant well. But the diff stops one step short: it makes the hook *run* without making its output *reach the user*, and that turns out to matter a lot.

### 1. The hook now runs, but its output and its prompts are captured and discarded — high

`pushBranchToRemote` still uses `cmd.CombinedOutput()`, and that buffer is only read to build an error string. Everything the pre-push hook says lands in it:

| what | where it writes |
| --- | --- |
| `[entire] Pushing N checkpoint ref(s) to origin...` | `manual_commit_push.go:491` → `os.Stderr` |
| `warnOPFCheckpointRefsWithheld` | `manual_commit_push.go:272` → `stderrWriter` = `os.Stderr` (`manual_commit_hooks.go:821`) |
| `askOPFPrompt`'s huh form | `uiform.New` → huh defaults to `os.Stdout` / `os.Stdin` |

Three consequences:

**(a)** On success the user sees nothing. `entire trail create` prints `Pushed branch X to origin` and that's it — the checkpoint sync this change exists to trigger is invisible.

**(b)** On the **git-refs** backend, an OPF failure calls `warnOPFCheckpointRefsWithheld`, returns false, and `PrePushFromGitHook` still returns nil — the push succeeds with the refs left queued. So trail create reports success while the checkpoints stay local. That is the original bug, unfixed, with its only warning now suppressed.

**(c)** The OPF prompt. `CanPromptInteractively()` decides purely from a `/dev/tty` probe (`interactive/interactive.go:55`) — it never looks at stdin or stdout. So for a human in a terminal with OPF on and `prompt_default` unset, `hasTTY` is true and `askOPFPrompt` renders a Bubble Tea form into a pipe with `/dev/null` for input. Whatever that resolves to decides whether the push aborts (`errOPFAbortedByUser`, `manual_commit_push.go:149`, git-branch) or the refs are withheld (git-refs).

Fix: stream rather than capture — `cmd.Stdout`/`cmd.Stderr` wired to the command's writers, exit status kept for the error. That's what "push like a user would" actually means.

Worth noting *why* this got missed: the dev loop ran through Pi, and `PI_CODING_AGENT` trips `isAgentSubprocessEnv()` → `hasTTY` false → OPF auto-runs with a progress line instead of a prompt. The human path is the one with no coverage.

### 2. The hard-failure path is new, untested, and its hint now misleads — medium

`prepareTrailCreateBranch:1126` treats a push failure as fatal: cleanup runs, trail creation aborts. Before this change the push could only fail on network/auth. Now **any** non-zero pre-push exit kills trail creation — Entire's OPF abort, or the user's own pre-push hook running tests or lint. Meanwhile the hint still reads:

```
- if this is an auth error, link your GitHub account and retry
- if this is a non-fast-forward, update branch %q from %q and retry
```

...with the real cause sitting in the captured buffer. Either widen the hint, or don't treat a hook rejection as a delivery failure at all.

A negative test is ~10 lines beside the new one: `pre-push` that `exit 1` → assert the error and that cleanup ran.

### 3. The 2-minute timeout now bounds hook work too — medium

`pushBranchToRemote` keeps `2*time.Minute`. That used to bound a network push; it now also bounds OPF re-redaction (~30s advertised, and the bootstrap case walks all unpushed history) plus the checkpoint ref pushes. On expiry `exec.CommandContext` kills git mid-hook. Either raise it or say why 2 minutes still holds.

### 4. `deleteBranchFromRemote` keeps `--no-verify`, undocumented — low

Line 2450. Probably correct — you don't want checkpoint sync on a branch delete — but the new comment asserts "This must run Git's pre-push hooks" without saying why its sibling must not. One clause there stops the next person removing it for consistency.

Related new state: if the push succeeds (hook publishes refs) and trail creation then fails, cleanup deletes the branch while the checkpoint refs stay published. Harmless, since they were meant to be pushed, but it's new.

### 5. Drop the `contexts_test.go` line — low

`t.Fatal` calls `runtime.Goexit()`, so the added `return` is unreachable and guards nothing. I ran `mise run lint` on clean main: **0 issues** — so it isn't silencing a linter either. And the commit carrying it is titled "Fix nil guard in contexts test", which describes something the line doesn't do. Unrelated file, no effect; cut it.

### What's right

- Correct fix, and the comment explains the invariant rather than just restating the code.
- The test isolates global git config via `testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv` (`initTrailCleanupRepo:349`) — without that, a developer carrying a global `core.hooksPath` gets a false failure.
- Asserting `$1 == "origin"` ties it to the remote resolution from `ed5f8e17c` instead of just "a hook ran".
- No recursion hazard: the checkpoint push itself passes `--no-verify` (`checkpoint/remote/git.go:434`).

### One coverage note

`TestGitPushWithHooks_SyncsCheckpointsToRemote` already exists in `integration_test/real_hook_push_test.go`, and `testenv.GitPushWithHooks` is right there. The new unit test asserts a proxy (some hook fired); an integration test asserting real checkpoint refs land after `trail create` would assert the actual claim. That session read `real_hook_push_test.go` and then didn't use it — it's the cheapest upgrade available here.

content.text:
No — three things, and the third is the one that makes the push non-negotiable.

**1. The ref has to exist before the create request.** `newTrailCreateRequest` sets `BranchAction = "link"` unconditionally whenever a branch is named (`trail_cmd.go:1219`). Per `dc40fb68c2e9`, without the branch on the remote the server "had no remote branch to anchor to and backfilled it at the base tip, producing local/remote/work drift while still printing 'Created trail'."

**2. Not just the ref — the commits.** The trail's `headSha` is the delivered tip (1219's is `a9e95a1b`). If the branch already exists on the remote but is behind, the push has to fast-forward it — that's what the non-fast-forward branch of the error hint is for. So it's a content delivery, not a ref creation.

**3. `-u` sets tracking.** Purely local, but it's what makes the next bare `git push` from that branch work — and, neatly, what lets `strategy.DeclaredPushRemoteForBranch` resolve on subsequent pushes, which is the machinery `ed5f8e17c` added.

## The point I think you're circling

Checkpoint publication is not a *purpose* of that push. It's a side effect of a hook the push happens to trigger. So the fix couples "publish checkpoints" to "deliver a branch" through a hook, on a push the user never typed, whose stdout is a buffer and whose stdin is `/dev/null`.

And the irony: the original commit had the right architecture and the wrong function. It *did* push Entire's data explicitly, on the very next lines —

```go
if err := strategy.PushTrailsBranch("origin"); err != nil {
```

— it just pushed the trails metadata branch instead of the checkpoint refs. The fix inverts that: rather than correcting the explicit call, it deletes the flag and adopts the hook as the mechanism.

I still think removing `--no-verify` is the better of the two. One code path, no drift, and the hook is the only thing that knows the whole push story — which refs are queued, which remote is elected, whether OPF applies, the policy sync. An explicit call would have to re-derive all of that and would rot.

But it's only right if the push is made to *be* a real push: streamed stdio, real stdin, and a timeout that accounts for hook work. Running the hook while keeping `CombinedOutput()` and a 2-minute budget is the half-measure that generates every finding in my review.

## One thing I checked that came out in the fix's favour

I worried the hook wouldn't fire when the branch is already on the remote at the same SHA — which would leave the most common flow (push your branch, *then* create the trail) unfixed. It does fire:

```
=== push 2 (already up to date, same SHA) ===
PRE-PUSH RAN remote=origin
Everything up-to-date
```

So the no-op push still syncs. That's the case that matters most, and it's covered.

content.text:
Distilled to what's worth saying on the trail:

## Main feedback

**The direction is right; the push just isn't a real push yet.** Dropping `--no-verify` is the correct fix and the new comment states the invariant well. But `pushBranchToRemote` still calls `CombinedOutput()` with nil stdin and a 2-minute budget, so the hook now runs blind: it can't print, can't prompt, and can't take as long as it needs.

**The sharp consequence — the named bug can still happen, silently.** On the git-refs backend, an OPF problem calls `warnOPFCheckpointRefsWithheld` and returns false, but `PrePushFromGitHook` still returns nil. The push succeeds, the refs stay queued, and the warning goes to `os.Stderr` — straight into the discarded buffer. So `entire trail create` prints `Pushed branch X to origin` while the checkpoints stay local. That's the exact failure this trail is named after, now with its only diagnostic suppressed.

Same root cause covers the rest: the `[entire] Pushing N checkpoint ref(s)` progress line is invisible on the happy path, and OPF's `huh` prompt renders into a pipe because `CanPromptInteractively()` decides from a `/dev/tty` probe that never looks at stdout or stdin.

**The ask:** wire `cmd.Stdout`/`cmd.Stderr` to the command's writers, give it real stdin, and raise the timeout to cover hook work (OPF advertises ~30s, and its bootstrap walks all unpushed history).

## Smaller, worth mentioning

- **The hard-fail hint now misleads.** A push failure aborts trail creation (`prepareTrailCreateBranch:1126`), and the hint only names auth and non-fast-forward. Any non-zero pre-push exit now lands there — including the user's own hook running tests. Untested, too: a `pre-push` that exits 1 is ~10 lines next to the new test.
- **Drop the `contexts_test.go` line.** `t.Fatal` calls `runtime.Goexit()`, so the `return` is unreachable. I ran `mise run lint` on clean main: 0 issues, so it isn't silencing anything either — and the commit carrying it is titled "Fix nil guard in contexts test".
- **Coverage.** `TestGitPushWithHooks_SyncsCheckpointsToRemote` already exists in `integration_test/real_hook_push_test.go`. The new unit test asserts a proxy (some hook fired); the real assertion — checkpoint refs land on the remote after `trail create` — is available for cheap.

## Worth crediting

- The hook fires even on `Everything up-to-date` (I verified), so the common flow — push your branch, then create the trail — is genuinely fixed.
- `testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv` in the test helper is doing real work; without it a global `core.hooksPath` gives a false failure.
- Asserting `$1 == "origin"` ties it to the remote resolution from `ed5f8e17c` rather than just "a hook ran".

One framing note if it comes up in discussion: the original commit actually had the right architecture and the wrong call — it pushed Entire's data explicitly via `strategy.PushTrailsBranch("origin")`, just the trails metadata branch instead of the checkpoint refs. Removing the flag is still the better answer (the hook is the only thing that knows the queued refs, the elected remote, OPF, and the policy sync), but it's worth saying so out loud so nobody later "restores" the explicit call.

Want me to post this on the trail?

trail create: stream the branch push so its hooks can be seen

Dropping --no-verify made the pre-push hook run, but the push was still
an internal subprocess: CombinedOutput() with nil stdin and a two-minute
budget. Two consequences, both of which defeat the point of running the
hook at all.

Entire's hook reports on stderr both when it pushes checkpoint refs and
when it withholds them, and on the git-refs backend it withholds them
while still exiting zero. With that output read only on failure, trail
create could print "Pushed branch" for a push that published nothing —
the failure this path exists to prevent, with its only diagnostic
discarded.

The OPF prompt became unanswerable in practice rather than skipped.
CanPromptInteractively() decides from a /dev/tty probe and never
consults stdio, so it still said yes; bubbletea falls back to /dev/tty
for prompt input when stdin is not a terminal, but has no such fallback
for output, which is unconditionally os.Stdout. The form rendered into
the captured buffer while reading real keystrokes, so the push blocked
on a prompt nobody could see.

stdout and stderr now stream to the caller's writers, and stdin is
inherited so git can prompt for credentials as on a push the user typed.
The returned error carries the exit status alone, since git's own message
has already reached the user.

The timeout goes to 10 minutes. It now covers the hook, and OPF is ~30s
in the steady state and bounded only by history on the first push after
a repo enables it; at two minutes exec would SIGKILL git mid-rewrite. A
bound remains because trail create is multi-step and a wedged push must
not hang it.

Because the push is a precondition for creating the trail, a hook that
says no now fails trail creation — Entire's own, or one the repo
installed for its own reasons. The hint offered only auth and
non-fast-forward, so it now names a rejected hook and points at the
output above. A test covers that path: the branch lands on neither side,
and the hook's reason reaches the caller.

deleteBranchFromRemote keeps --no-verify, now with a comment saying why,
so the asymmetry is not read as an oversight: it retracts a branch on a
failed create, so there is nothing to publish, and running checkpoint
sync while unwinding is work in the wrong direction.

content.text:
Done — two commits on top of `dip/fix-trail-create-checkpoint-sync`, and the branch now touches only the two trail files relative to `main`.

## What went in

**`4fd576d58` — stream the branch push so its hooks can be seen**

- `pushBranchToRemote` now takes the caller's writers and sets `cmd.Stdout`/`cmd.Stderr` instead of `CombinedOutput()`; stdin is inherited. Error carries the exit status only, since git's own message now reaches the user.
- Timeout 2min → 10min, behind a named `trailBranchPushTimeout` with the reasoning attached.
- The failure hint gains a "a pre-push hook rejected the push" bullet — the cause the change made reachable.
- `deleteBranchFromRemote` keeps `--no-verify`, now with a comment saying why, so the asymmetry doesn't read as an oversight.
- Tests: the existing hook test now also asserts the hook's output reaches the caller's stderr, plus a new `TestPrepareTrailCreateBranchFailsWhenPrePushHookRejects` (branch lands on neither side, hint names the hook, hook's reason reaches the caller). Both pass; the rejection test also exercises `cleanupCreatedTrailBranch`, which had no coverage.

**`035af7d31` — revert "Fix nil guard in contexts test"**

`mise run check` passed in full (unit + integration + race + build + both canary legs, 240s).

## One correction to what I told you earlier

I said the OPF prompt would be "at best invisible". Reading bubbletea, it's worse and more specific: `tea.go:1016` falls back to `/dev/tty` for **input** when stdin isn't a terminal, but output is unconditionally `os.Stdout` with no such fallback (`tea.go:625`). So under the old code the form was reading real keystrokes while rendering into the discarded buffer — a push that blocks on a prompt the user cannot see, not one that silently defaults. The commit message and the code comment both state the verified mechanism rather than my first guess.

## One item I did not do, and why

The integration test I called "available for cheap" isn't. `resolveTrailRemote` (`trail_cmd.go`) hard-requires origin to be a supported forge:

```go
if forge == "" {
    return "", "", "", errors.New("origin remote is not on a forge supported by Entire trails (supported: github.com)")
}
```

So `entire trail create` can't be driven against a local bare remote. Making it work needs origin as a fake `github.com` URL plus a second remote and `remote.pushDefault` for the push — which then drags in the checkpoint-sync election, since origin would be the elected remote and the checkpoint push would target github.com unless the pre-push capture path steers it first. That's real new scaffolding with a live risk of passing for the wrong reason, so I stopped rather than build it on my own judgment.

The composition is covered by two tests meeting in the middle — `TestPrepareTrailCreateBranchRunsPrePushHook` (this path runs the hook, right remote) and `TestGitPushWithHooks_SyncsCheckpointsToRemote` (the real hook lands checkpoints, both backends). Worth saying on the trail as a known gap; tell me if you want the harness built and I'll do it.

Nothing is pushed. Want me to push to the branch, and post the review as a trail comment?

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

content.text:
Cleanup pass done, committed as `e55fb20c3`. `mise run lint` clean, `mise run test:ci` green (56 canary + 4 external, full unit/integration).

## Fixed

**The timeout comment was factually wrong** (altitude). I'd written that the hook's worst case is "bounded only by history" on a first OPF run. It isn't: both rewrite paths make *exactly one* shell-out per push (`manual_commit_opf_rewrite.go:367`, `manual_commit_opf_refs.go:128`), bounded by `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.timeout_seconds` — 30s default (`redact/opf.go:61`) — and an oversized first run is *rejected* by `BootstrapTooLargeError`/`OPFRawBytesTooLargeError` rather than allowed to run long. The real unbounded wait is the OPF prompt waiting on a person, which is what 10 minutes is actually sized for. The comment now says that, and records the limitation it implies: `timeout_seconds` is validated only as `>= 0` (`settings.go:1522`), so a larger configured value gets truncated and git is killed mid-rewrite.

**Duplicated rationale** (simplification). The doc comment's closing paragraph said the same thing as the inline comment eight lines below it. Dropped the doc copy; the inline one sits at the `return` it explains.

**Replaced it with the property the fix actually rests on** (efficiency). `os/exec` passes an `*os.File`'s fd straight to the child — so the hook inherits the terminal — while any other `io.Writer` gets an `os.Pipe` and the child's stdout stops being a tty. That's *why* streaming makes the prompt visible, and it holds only because nothing on the path to `trail create` calls `SetOut`/`SetErr`. A pager on the root command would silently undo the whole fix. Nothing else recorded that.

**Hook scripts → backtick raw strings** (simplification). The concatenated `\\n`/`\"` form was the outlier; `setup_test.go`, `explain_test.go`, `session_adopt_test.go` and `external_test.go` all use raw strings for shell scripts.

## Skipped

- **Deriving the timeout from `timeout_seconds`** — the deeper fix the altitude agent proposed. It's a behaviour change, so out of scope for a cleanup pass; recorded in the comment instead so whoever hits it knows the fix.
- **`gitBranchExistsTrailTest` → `testutil.BranchExists`** — real duplication, but it predates this diff and is used by sibling tests in the same file. File-wide follow-up.
- **`out` parameter unexercised by tests** — neither hook script writes to stdout, so only the `errOut` path is asserted. Coverage gap, not a simplification; the parameter itself is justified (a hook's own TUI renders to stdout).
- **Error-hint string shape** and the **single-use `trailBranchPushTimeout` const** — both confirmed as house style by two agents independently. Left alone.

Reuse and efficiency both came back clean otherwise. Still nothing pushed — three commits sitting on `dip/fix-trail-create-checkpoint-sync` locally.

content.text:
Five findings. Two were right and I've fixed them; the High one is wrong on its stated mechanism.

## The High finding is wrong — `01M1Y6WD9BEP`

> Git push hooks run **after** the network transfer, so a hook rejection leaves an orphaned branch on the remote.

That premise is false for `pre-push` — rejecting is the whole point of it. Tested directly:

```
--- push (hook rejects) ---
    hook ran, rejecting
    error: failed to push some refs to '../origin.git'
--- refs on the remote afterwards ---
    ref count: 0
```

The branch never lands. `TestPrepareTrailCreateBranchFailsWhenPrePushHookRejects`, already on the branch, asserts exactly this and passes.

There *is* a narrow residual behind it: `cleanupCreatedTrailBranch` is called with a hardcoded `false` for `remotePushed` (`trail_cmd.go:1140`), so if the push landed refs and *then* errored — a SIGKILL at the timeout is the only realistic route — the remote branch is orphaned. That `false` predates this trail, and the suggested `state.RemotePushed || existedOnRemote` would be wrong: `existedOnRemote` means the user already had the branch, so cleanup would delete a branch we didn't create. Not fixing it here — narrow, pre-existing, and changing cleanup semantics is a call for the branch owner.

## Fixed — `01M1XX4E1ENC` (stdin), right in direction

I'd written that inheriting stdin lets git prompt for credentials. That justification doesn't hold: `git push` has no `--stdin`, the hook gets git's ref-list pipe rather than ours, the OPF prompt reads `/dev/tty` via bubbletea's fallback, and git's credential prompt uses `/dev/tty`/askpass. So the only effect was replacing an immediate EOF with a real blocking read — an agent-driven `trail create` could hang for ten minutes instead of failing fast. Dropped; stdin stays at `/dev/null`.

## Fixed — `01M1Y5JYARYN`, even though it's marked dismissed

It's technically right, and there's a repo-idiomatic fix nobody applied. `exec.CommandContext`'s default `Cancel` kills only the direct child — and the pre-push hook is a *grandchild*. So a timeout orphaned it: `trail create` returns an error while a detached hook keeps rewriting checkpoint refs behind it. Now using `execx.TerminateOnCancel`, which kills the process group and sets `WaitDelay`.

The finding's literal complaint — SIGKILL corrupting a mid-ref-write — has no fix at this layer, and I said so in the comment rather than implying otherwise. But an orphaned writer nobody is waiting for is strictly worse than a stopped one.

## Already addressed

- `01M1GQEGKZ40` (contexts_test `return` not needed) — exactly what `035af7d31` reverts. Genuinely fixed, still open.
- `01M1GPJ2D0GH` (hardcoded 2-minute timeout) — addressed by `trailBranchPushTimeout`; already dismissed.

Committed as `adc2d6fe0`. `mise run lint` clean, `test:ci` green, and `GOOS=windows go vet` passes — worth checking here because `execx`'s `killProcessGroupOnCancel` is a no-op on Windows.

Not pushed, and I haven't written anything to the trail. Want me to push, resolve `01M1GQEGKZ40`, and reply on the High one with the repro?

Stefan Haubold <stefan@entire.io>
Mon Sep 7 17:11:41 2026 +0200

Say what the push timeout actually kills, and what a pipe would cost

The known-limitation note on trailBranchPushTimeout claimed expiry kills git
mid-rewrite. It kills git, but not the rewrite: CommandContext's default Cancel
is Process.Kill() on the child PID, no Setpgid is set, and the OPF re-redaction
and ref CAS-updates run in the pre-push hook — a grandchild. The hook is
orphaned, not interrupted, so the StatusWalkBudget failure mode (SIGKILL on the
process holding the lock) does not transfer here. Record the orphan as the cost
that is actually being accepted, and why killing the group would be worse.

Second note: the *os.File requirement is load-bearing for more than the tty.
With a pipe interposed, Cmd.Wait blocks on its copy goroutine until every
holder of the write end closes, an orphaned hook holds one, and WaitDelay is
unset — so a pager on the root command would leave this call unbounded, which
is the one thing the timeout exists to prevent.

Comments only; no behaviour change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

+// is sent. The OPF re-redaction and the checkpoint ref CAS-updates do not run

+// which execs `entire hooks pre-push`). So the hook is orphaned, not
+// interrupted: expiry cannot leave a half-rewritten ref or a stale lock the way
+// StatusWalkBudget's SIGKILL can, because that one kills the process holding

+// used to describe, which is the worse of the two.

@@ -2514,6 +2531,12 @@ const trailBranchPushTimeout = 10 * time.Minute

 //

+// Cmd.Wait blocks on its copy goroutine until every holder of the write end
+// closes it — and an orphaned hook (see trailBranchPushTimeout) holds one.
+// WaitDelay is unset, so that wait has no ceiling: the timeout above would stop
+// bounding this call at all, which is the one thing it exists to do.
+//
 // stdin is inherited so git can prompt for credentials as on a push the user
 // typed. It does not reach the hook, which git hands a pipe carrying the ref
 // list — that is why the prompt's input path goes through /dev/tty above.

trail create: stop inheriting stdin for the branch push

Addresses a finding on the trail. The justification the comment gave —
git prompting for credentials as it would on a push the user typed —
does not hold. git push has no --stdin mode; git's own credential prompt
uses /dev/tty or askpass; the OPF prompt reads /dev/tty via bubbletea's

read. A non-interactive trail create — an agent whose stdin is a
long-lived pipe rather than a closed fd — could park on a prompt until
trailBranchPushTimeout instead of failing fast. Left at /dev/null, which
is where it was before the streaming change.

Deliberately does not touch cancellation: the orphaned-hook cost is
recorded as accepted in trailBranchPushTimeout's note, and killing the
process group would reverse that decision, not refine it.
